name: Dental implants

image.caption: Dr.Ihab Hanna teaching in a dental implants live surgeries Course

lead: Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result. A titanium or zirconia post is set in the jawbone and topped with a crown, bridge or denture, so a gap is filled with a tooth that looks and works like the original.

The post bonds to bone through osseointegration, then supports the prosthetic tooth after healing. Reported survival is about 93 to 98 percent at five years or more in healthy tissue. On looksmaxxing forums people also ask whether implants and bone grafts can thicken the jaw or build chin projection, but reference sources describe implants as tooth replacements and do not describe such effects.

paras: Placement is oral surgery done in stages, with healing time before the crown is fitted. Rough surfaces and coatings are designed to speed bone attachment. People plan implants around gaps, failing teeth and the final shape of the smile.

Complications include infection, loosening, fracture, nerve injury and peri-implantitis (bone loss around the implant), which are more likely with smoking, poor hygiene and diabetes. It is a surgical, hard-to-reverse treatment.

angle.text: Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result: a titanium root is set in bone and a crown fitted on top. Forum posters also ask about thickening the jaw or building up a recessed chin with implants and grafts, but that use is not described in reference sources.

lead: A dental implant is a prosthetic fixture, most often made of titanium or zirconia, that is anchored in the jaw bone to support a crown, bridge or denture. Modern implants rely on osseointegration, a close bond between bone and the implant material [1]. They are used mainly to replace missing teeth.

In looksmaxxing forums, implants are mostly discussed as a way to fill gaps, and occasionally with the question of whether an implant plus bone grafting can thicken or reshape the jaw. Encyclopedic sources describe implants as tooth-replacement devices and do not describe them as changing facial or jaw shape [1].

Survival rates in healthy tissue are reported at roughly 93 to 98 percent at five years or more, with complications such as peri-implantitis and mechanical problems reported over longer follow-up [1].
infobox: Commercially pure titanium (most common); zirconia ceramic [1]
About 93 to 98 percent in healthy tissue [1]

paras: The implant is placed first and a prosthesis is attached after healing. Indications listed include single-tooth replacement, implant-supported bridges, implant-supported overdentures for toothless jaws, orthodontic anchorage and retention of facial prostheses [1]. Surgery typically involves exposing bone, drilling progressively wider holes with cooling, placing the implant and later attaching an abutment and crown [1].

Loading may be immediate, early (about 1 to 12 weeks) or delayed (over 3 months) [1]. Bone and gum can shrink after tooth extraction, which is why bone grafts or sinus lifts are sometimes used before placement [1][2].

Titanium alloy is used mostly for abutments and screws, while most implant bodies use commercially pure titanium. Zirconia implants exist but long-term data are limited [1]. Surface roughness and osteoconductive coatings are described as favouring bone anchoring and faster biological fixation [3], and a chemically modified rough titanium surface was reported to enhance bone apposition in a preclinical study [4].

A widely cited 1986 review proposed criteria for judging long-term success of implants [5]. A multi-centre prospective study of 2,359 non-submerged implants reported 8-year life table results [6]. Reported figures in a general reference include integration failure of 1 to 6 percent in the first six months and long-term success without complications of 52 to 76 percent at 16 to 20 years [1].
Use has risen in the United States from 0.7 percent of patients missing a tooth in 1999 to 2000 to 5.7 percent in 2015 to 2016 [1].

Reported surgical complications include infection, bleeding and injury to nerves, sinuses or vessels, and failure to integrate is more likely with smoking or poor health [1]. For single crowns at five years, one summary lists screw or abutment loosening in about 12.7 percent and implant fracture of 0.14 percent [1].

Peri-implant mucositis is reversible inflammation, while peri-implantitis involves bone loss and can lead to implant removal. A 2017 consensus workshop defined these conditions [7]. Peri-implantitis prevalence of about 9.7 percent at five years is cited for single crowns, with higher values in some studies [1]. Bisphosphonate-related exposed bone (osteonecrosis) of the jaws has been described as a risk factor consideration in jaw procedures [8].

Users on looksmax.org have asked whether a molar implant with bone grafting would thicken a jaw that is less dense on one side [9][10], whether jaw surgery can be done after implants [11], whether implants can improve a recessed chin [12], and whether implants damage the jaw [13]. The threads are questions, and the reference sources reviewed here do not describe implants as altering jaw or chin shape.

Human studies of implants are extensive. Registered trials include a 39-year follow-up of the world's first single dental implants [14], a trial of marginal bone around implants with different surface treatments supporting mandibular overdentures [15], a randomised comparison of flap designs over three years [16], a study of implants in patients with Sjogren's syndrome [17], and a randomised trial of materials in full-arch prosthetics [18]. These studies address tooth replacement and bone levels, not facial appearance. Treatment of peri-implant disease and extraction-socket changes have also been examined [7][2].
